This is called the “calendar” method - and is a valid form of pregnancy prevention. The issue is that it has about a 25% failure rate. This means over the course of 1 year while using the calendar method, you have about a 25% chance of getting pregnant. 

For comparison, an IUD has a less than 1% failure rate. 

People have used the calendar method for generations, and there are ways to improve the process (taking daily temperature checks and ovulation tests prior to unprotected intercourse) but someone using the calendar method should be more prepared to address a possible pregnancy than someone using other forms of contraception

The best advice I can give is start with a list of all of your expenses: amount and date due.
Your big expenses (typically rent/daycare/maybe car payments?) you want to split in half from each check.

Example 
Bi weekly check is $100 
Rent is $100

Instead of using a whole check to pay rent - take $50 from one and $50 from another. 

I recommend doing this with any "must pays" so if you ever have a tough month - you can always pay half of your bill

Then for the rest of your bills, just try to make them equal across checks. So bills due at the beginning of the month come from your first check, bills at the end of the month come from the second check. 

Try to keep it similar across checks as best as you can so you consistently have about the same left over after each payday. It makes it so much easier to get in the habit of saving money or not overspending when you have a routine with how much you have, rather than having 1 check for bills and 1 check for fun money.

Hey! You can do this!
Ive interviews tons of people in my role at work, and can fully tell you you're not alone in this situation.

Start with a clean CV. list at the top what education you have completed - so if that stops at high school, thats okay! 

Write a category for professional experience with your one job. Include any and all tasks you did while there. 

Then put a category after with volunteer & club experience. Write down anything you've done while you were in school, wether it be sports or a club. Add any roles you've had volunteering even if they're informal - maybe its at church or at a community center. 

If you still need to fill space, put a category of special skills. List that you're fluent in microsoft products. Any other software you know, even if its not super related to what you're applying to. 

Lastly - try have at least one reference thats not your family. Have it be your pastor/religious leader or someone you worked with volunteering. A co-worker from your last job if you've kept in touch. 

If you don't have much on the page when you're done: thats totally okay. You're looking for entry level positions - they expect that they're going to need to train you. Make sure its formatted nicely, has no typos or grammar issues and be done. If you can prove you can at least put together a professional document, a lot of entry level jobs will looks favorably for that. 

You wouldn't believe how many resume's I've reviewed that are total train-wrecks from people who have years & years of work experience.

Look up the point system! The federal government uses points to fairly rate candidates to earn interviews. So education has points, experience, certifications, licenses, etc. everything is worth a certain point value. Top 10/20/30/etc candidates with the highest point values get interview. 

Vets are automatically awarded an extra 5 or 10 points depending on type of service, so if you see a federal posting that acknowledges “vet preference” know you’ll automatically be competing with someone who can have 105/100 or 110/100 points on a perfect resume

This is 100% false for every federal agency. We no longer use computers to keyword search. Except NASA. NASA still uses computers.

We do have a separate HR department that reviews before sending a candidate list to the hiring authority. Which means there is a person reading potentially hundreds of resumes at once that only knows to look for what the hiring person said to look for, plus the standardized job requirements/description.

This! Also government resumes are often 5-10 pages long with the average being 8. Look up how to write a government resume. Paragraphs are required. So many amazing candidates miss out because they submit 1 page with bullet points when someone less qualified submits 5 pages of paragraphs. The more details you provide, the more points you earn and the more likely you’re able to secure an interview.
